description: Solo team based in Spain. I am interested in disaster preparation and public health, and I build tools by directing AI coding assistants. This project turns 25 years of NASA fire detections into a burning calendar for a town, and into dates by which nurses, schools and patients should get ready for the smoke season. Not looking for more members this year; feedback from people in respiratory care, schools or fire services is welcome.
summary: Burn calendar: breathe early is a web app that harmonizes NASA FIRMS hotspots from MODIS (2000–2025) and VIIRS (2012–2025) into one consistent burning-activity calendar for any area the user picks, and turns that calendar into weeks of notice for the people who care for those with breathing problems. For a chosen town it shows which weeks usually burn, how few of the official burning window's weeks actually carry the burning, and prints one-page notices that say what to do before those weeks and how many days ahead: for a respiratory nurse working with the community pharmacist, for patients and parents, and for schools, care homes and dialysis units. The app also tests itself: each past year is judged using earlier years only, and the result is shown on screen (it gets the season right, not the week). It is not a smoke forecast: for the day itself it points to the official QUEPAR app and the regional air-quality network. Our first area is the Albufera, Valencia (Spain): the 2026 campaign allows rice-straw burning over about 15 weeks, but near Sueca the satellites saw the burning between early October and mid-November in every year from 2016 to 2025, and in October 2024 smoke kept about 700 pupils in El Saler indoors.
details:
What it does. The app answers the challenge in two parts and adds one use on top.

  1. Harmonization. MODIS and VIIRS hotspots cannot be compared directly: VIIRS pixels are 375 m against ~1 km for MODIS, and VIIRS detects many more small fires. The app (a) applies the same filters to both (FIRMS type 0 = presumed vegetation fire; low-confidence detections removed), (b) counts the same unit for both — unique sensor-day-0.01° "hotspot cells", which removes most of the pixel-size effect — and (c) cross-calibrates on the 2012–2025 overlap with a ratio k = VIIRS ÷ MODIS, recomputed live for the area the user selects. The harmonized series is MODIS × k before 2012 and VIIRS from 2012, so the sensor of origin no longer matters to the calendar. Because the ratio depends on the kind of fire (Albufera rice area k ≈ 4, whole province k ≈ 1.5), the local ratio is used only when the local overlap holds (at least 30 MODIS cells and year-to-year r ≥ 0.6), otherwise the province-wide ratio; the user can force either. Leave-one-year-out check shown in the app: Valencia province r = 0.97, median single-year error 20%; Albufera r = 0.87, 27%.
  2. Burning-activity calendar. A year × month grid of harmonized hotspots (2001–2025) with an accessible colour ramp (cividis), the selected year against the median of the other years, key figures, a map with every hotspot, and CSV downloads of the hotspots for any date range and of the harmonized monthly series. The user picks a town or clicks the map, and sets the radius.
  3. Breathe early: prepare before the season. For each week of the year the app computes the share of past years with burning within the radius. It then shows what the calendar adds to the official window: the 2026 campaign allows rice-straw burning from 16 September to 31 December at the latest (about 15 weeks); near Sueca (15 km, 2016–2025) 6 of those weeks carry 80% of the in-window hotspots, looking back; near El Palmar, 5 weeks. A built-in test then asks whether that would have worked as a forecast: each year from 2011 to 2025 is judged with the weeks the calendar would have flagged on 1 January of that year, from the ten years before it. Near Sueca, flagged weeks burned 25% of the time against 20% for a week picked blind, and the core weeks picked in advance carried about half of the next year's burning, not 80%. The calendar knows the season, not the week. The running year is in the calendar too, to 2 November 2026: near Sueca 15 hotspots so far against a median of 24 to the same date, and 6 since the official window opened on 16 September against a median of 15 for the same dates over 2016–2025. 2026 is a season the calendar had never seen and is not used to choose weeks: so far 7 of its 12 flagged weeks burned, and 7 of its 11 burning weeks had been flagged. So the default heads-up level was lowered from 50% to 30% of years (a choice made after seeing the test, and stated on screen), and the notices speak about the season (near Sueca, 17 September to 11 November). The tab opens with one picture, "When to act": the year as a ribbon with the usual season marked, and one pin per group at the season's start minus the days that group needs to get ready. From the main season or the next window, it writes one-page notices, two side by side, each with its own lead time (adjustable assumptions):
    • A · respiratory nurse in primary care, with the community pharmacist as outreach partner (28 days ahead): review action plans and inhaler technique, check that patients have the medicines already prescribed to them, find the people who cannot get clean air at home, use the pharmacy counter for reminders.
    • B · patient or parent (7 days ahead): collect what is prescribed, carry the reliever, know your action plan (ask your nurse or pharmacist), close windows and avoid hard exercise on days you see or smell smoke.
    • C · school, care home or dialysis unit (21 days ahead): filters and air cleaners ordered in time, one clean-air room, indoor alternatives for sport and outings, who checks QUEPAR and the air-quality network on burning days. The app states on screen what the calendar is — the usual burning season from satellite fire detections — and what it is not: a smoke forecast. FIRMS sees fires, not what people breathe. For the day itself it points to QUEPAR, the Generalitat Valenciana and CEAM app that tells farmers the hours when burning is allowed, and to the regional air-quality network (GVA Aire). It does not replace them. An optional upwind filter keeps only hotspots upwind of the town on that day (NASA POWER daily wind).

Evidence shown in the app (checked sources only). Rice-straw burning and asthma admissions, Butte County, California, 1983–1992: RR 1.23 on days with more than 499 acres burned (Jacobs et al. 1997). Reliever dispensing in British Columbia: about 6% more salbutamol per 10 µg/m³ PM2.5 (Elliott et al. 2013). Ambulance calls for breathing problems within one hour of smoke (Yao et al. 2020). The local case: in October 2024 burning around the Albufera reached about four times the usual daily peak over two days, and about 700 pupils of the El Saler schools stayed inside with windows shut (elDiario.es, 12–13 Oct 2024). Inhaler demand appears only as an optional, labelled assumption based on Elliott et al.; more demand is documented, running out is not.

Benefits. Health and education planners get a consistent 25-year fire history for their own area and a narrow, dated season to prepare for, instead of a 15-week legal window. Nurses, schools and care homes get the weeks of notice that preparation needs; patients get plain advice at the right time.

What we hope to achieve. Test the notices with one primary-care team and one school in El Saler; check the season against air-quality measurements; add NOAA-20/21 VIIRS; send the notices by email to opted-in centres.

Limits we state openly. Fires seen from space are not smoke; no local study links Albufera burning days to health visits, and the app does not claim one. One ratio per area does not model fire size, season or overpass time; single-year errors of 20–40% are normal. The wind comes from one grid point. The app does not claim to prevent illness: it addresses the "prepare before the usual burning weeks" link.

Tools and languages. Python 3 standard library (data build and validation), plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript (no framework, no build step), SVG charts drawn by hand, Leaflet 1.9.4 with OpenStreetMap tiles. Runs from a local web server or as a single self-contained HTML file.
